passage:
Deepika noticed her parents lowering their voices whenever she came in. One evening she asked her mother gently, "Has something changed?" Her mother sighed and told her that Papa's income had dropped since the factory cut hours. The vague worry became a clear problem with limits, and Deepika felt steadier for knowing.

Next morning she asked Parul Ma'am, the class teacher, what help existed with fees. Parul Ma'am told her about a scholarship form. Deepika gathered certificates with her parents over the weekend and handed in the application days before the last date.

Omkar, in the next row, had heard similar things at home and said nothing. He joked with friends, smiled, and told his mother school was fine. His marks slipped and he stopped sleeping well. His parents, unaware of his load, could not reassure him or share it.

To help with costs, Deepika began tutoring younger children. A month later she was falling asleep over her own notes. She and her parents cut the tutoring to two evenings and looked for another source of aid, agreeing that her studies came first.

qa.q: Why had Papa's income dropped?
qa.a: The factory cut hours.

qa.q: How did Deepika's way of handling the worry differ from Omkar's, and what happened?
qa.a: Deepika asked questions, applied for help, and later rebalanced her tutoring with her parents, while Omkar hid his worry and his marks slipped without his parents knowing.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling behind the jokes?
qa.a: Worry and strain, hidden behind smiles.

qa.q: What could Omkar do?
qa.a: Omkar could tell his parents or a teacher what he is worried about so they can help him share it.

grounding: Four teen approaches to a family financial squeeze: asking openly, seeking scholarships, hiding the worry, and rebalancing after overwork.

passage:
Three new children started in Class 6 on the same Monday.

Vidya spent the first days watching. She noticed which bench filled first, who shared erasers, and which game the girls near the tap played at recess. By Thursday she knew whom she wanted to walk up to.

Ravi strolled up to some boys eating lunch on day one. "Hi, I'm Ravi. We moved from Kanpur. Can I join your game?" A boy tossed him the ball and said, "You're on my team."

Sonali sat at the end of a bench with her lunch box, hoping someone would ask her over. Classmates glanced at her and assumed she liked being alone, so nobody came. Each day, the bench felt longer.

Farida spent her first week telling everyone about her big house, her trips and her cousin's cricket bat. Around her, conversations faded. On Friday she saw two girls stop talking as she came near. That weekend she thought about it. On Monday she asked a girl, "What do you play at recess?" and listened. By Wednesday she was told, "Come and sit with us."

qa.q: Where had Ravi moved from?
qa.a: Ravi had moved from Kanpur.

qa.q: How did Farida's first week differ from Ravi's, and what did she change?
qa.a: Farida talked about herself and conversations faded, while Ravi introduced himself and asked to join a game; Farida later began asking questions and listening and was invited to sit with the group.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling as the bench felt longer?
qa.a: Lonely, and hoping for an invitation.

qa.q: How could a classmate help Sonali?
qa.a: A classmate could walk over, say hello and invite her to join a game.

grounding: Four approaches to being new at school: watching first, introducing yourself, waiting alone, and changing after bragging fails.

passage:
Rajni sat on the kitchen floor. Her ball had rolled away. "Amma," she said. "Amma." She pointed at the ball. Her mother kept chopping vegetables. "Amma!" The fourth time, her mother looked, smiled, and rolled the ball back.

In the next room, Tarun wanted his father, who was looking at his phone. Tarun babbled. Nothing. He tapped the table. His father's eyes stayed on the screen. Tarun carried over his cup and held it up, and his father's head lifted. "Cup?" he said. After that, Tarun brought his cup every time.

Baljeet once cried very loudly and his mother ran to him. Since then, whenever she was busy at the stove, he screamed at the top of his lungs. She came each time, but started to answer only when it was loud, and the crying got louder.

Later that week, Rajni called "Amma" from across the room, and her mother, on a call, did not turn. Rajni thought. Then she got up, walked over, put both hands on her mother's knee and looked up. Her mother put the phone down.

qa.q: What did Tarun carry over to his father?
qa.a: Tarun carried over his cup.

qa.q: How did Baljeet's method of getting attention differ from Rajni's change of plan, and what did each lead to?
qa.a: Baljeet kept crying at full volume, so his mother answered only to loudness and the crying grew, while Rajni walked over and put her hands on her mother's knee, which brought her mother's attention without shouting.

qa.q: What was Tarun probably feeling when his father looked up?
qa.a: Pleased and relieved that the cup had finally worked.

qa.q: How could Baljeet's mother respond?
qa.a: She could go to him at a calm moment and answer quiet requests like pointing, so that shouting is not needed.

grounding: Four toddler approaches to getting a caregiver's attention: calling and pointing, trial and error, repeating loud crying, and moving closer.

passage:
Sachin wanted to learn chess. He picked Tuesday and Saturday evenings, one hour each, right after homework, and told his family at dinner: "That's my chess time." His sister stopped asking him to play cards on those days.

Jasleen started drawing with only ten minutes a day. She thought a tiny habit that carried on beat a big plan that fizzled after three days. By the end of a month, her sketchbook was half full.

Lokesh spent a whole week on a rainbow timetable for painting and a trip to buy brushes, paints and three sizes of paper. He pinned the timetable above his bed and admired it. At the end of the week, the paper was still white, and he had not painted a stroke.

Mira painted every afternoon, until exams came near. She cut it to Sunday mornings only, and wrote on her calendar, "Full time again after the last paper." She kept her brush wet on Sundays, and the painting stayed alive.

qa.q: Which evenings did Sachin set aside for chess?
qa.a: He set aside Tuesday and Saturday evenings.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh's week produce no painting while Jasleen's and Mira's routines continued?
qa.a: Lokesh spent the week planning and buying supplies without painting, while Jasleen kept a tiny daily habit and Mira cut down to Sundays during exams instead of quitting.

qa.q: What might Lokesh be feeling at the end of the week?
qa.a: A bit embarrassed and disappointed, since the paper was still white despite all the preparation.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do next?
qa.a: Lokesh could paint for ten minutes today with what he already has, and adjust the timetable later.

grounding: Four approaches to a hobby routine: a fixed slot, starting small, planning without starting, and reducing time during exams.

passage:
On Saturday morning, three rooms needed tidying.

Tushar looked around and said, "Books first." He put the books on the shelf. "Then toys." They went in the box. "Then clothes," and the clothes went into the basket. Each kind went by itself, and the floor came back.

Zainab had a rule her mother helped her make: "If it has wheels, it goes in the blue box." She picked up a car, a truck and her scooter, and put them in the blue box without asking anyone whether each one belonged.

Jagdish stood at the door and saw toys on the floor, on the bed, under the chair. He walked into the middle of the room, sat down, and picked up a wooden train. Chug, chug. By lunchtime the train had crossed the carpet twice, and nothing had gone into a box.

qa.q: What went in the blue box?
qa.a: Things with wheels went in the blue box: a car, a truck and a scooter.

qa.q: How did Jagdish's way of facing the mess differ from Tushar's and Zainab's?
qa.a: Tushar and Zainab used an order or a rule that made each next step clear, while Jagdish sat down to play with one toy and nothing got put away.

qa.q: What might Jagdish be feeling when he sees toys everywhere?
qa.a: Overwhelmed and unsure where to begin, so he turns to something familiar.

qa.q: How could an adult help Jagdish?
qa.a: An adult could start with him on one small kind of thing, like the wheeled toys, and let him finish it.

grounding: Three approaches to tidying a room at ages four to six: a step list, an if-then rule, and giving up when overwhelmed.

passage:
Keerthana, running for school captain, went from class to class with a notebook. Canteen queues that ate half of recess, footballs gone flat, the library closing at three: she wrote down what she heard and built her platform on those three things instead of promising "a better school."

She wrote a speech that would take two minutes: one promise, a shorter canteen queue, and one story about waiting so long she got two bites of lunch. She read it to the mirror and to Kavitha, timed it, and cut the filler until it ran a hundred and ten seconds.

Gurleen, everyone's friend, did not bother. "They'll vote for me," he said, and made no plan. While he chatted at the gate, his rivals visited more classes and told them exactly what they would do. When the votes were counted, Gurleen lost by a few, with a great deal of goodwill and no proposals.

The next morning he walked up to Keerthana, shook her hand, and asked, "What did I miss?" She told him. Then he said, "Can I lead the canteen committee with you?" They started with the queue.

qa.q: What did Keerthana build her platform on?
qa.a: She built it on the canteen queues, the flat footballs and the library closing at three.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's campaign succeed where Gurleen's failed?
qa.a: Keerthana asked classmates what they needed and practised a clear speech, while Gurleen relied on goodwill and made no plan; afterwards he asked her for feedback and offered to help with the canteen.

qa.q: What was Gurleen probably feeling when the votes were counted?
qa.a: Disappointed and surprised, since he had expected his friends to vote for him.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do to prepare next time?
qa.a: Gurleen could talk to more classes, find out their concerns and write a clear plan.

grounding: Four approaches to a school election: finding out what voters need, rehearsing a speech, relying on popularity, and learning from a loss.
